transcript.text: microwve plate wont go round anymore, food hot on one side cold on other. still heats tho

Uneven heating is exactly what you'd expect when the plate stops turning. The food sits still, so it gets hot spots and cold spots. Because it still heats, the heating side is very likely fine. This is almost always a simple mechanical issue with the turntable drive. 1. The glass plate has slipped off its drive, the roller ring underneath is dirty or dislodged, or a large dish is catching the sides. This is very common and free to fix.
2. The small plastic coupler in the middle, the three-pronged piece the plate sits on, has cracked or worn its grooves. 3. 1. Lift out the glass plate and the roller ring. Wipe the ring's wheels and the cavity floor, and remove any food or crumbs. Look at the coupler in the middle for cracks or rounded-off edges. Refit the ring, then sit the plate so the grooves underneath lock onto the coupler. It should drop slightly into place. If it was off, dirty or jammed, that was probably the whole problem.
2. Put a cup of water in and run it for a minute. If the plate now turns, you're sorted.
3. If it still won't turn, take the glass plate off, leaving the coupler in place, and run it again with a cup of water on the floor of the microwave. Watch the coupler. That usually means a cheap replacement coupler. If the coupler doesn't move at all and there's no sound, the turntable motor is the likely culprit. If it does come down to the motor, it sits underneath the cavity and normally needs the casing opened. Microwaves hold dangerous voltages inside even when unplugged, so that's an engineer job, not DIY. On an older or cheaper microwave, compare the repair cost with buying a new one. What do you see when you run it with the plate lifted out?

ran it with just a cup of water, the little 3 pronged plastic bit in the middle wobbles and doesnt really turn. the metal shaft under it looks like it moves a bit. also theres a crack in the plastic piece and the hole in the middle looks rounded

That points strongly at the coupler, the three-pronged plastic piece. The centre hole fits over a shaped metal shaft from the motor. Once that hole is rounded off and the plastic is cracked, the shaft just spins inside it, so the coupler wobbles instead of being driven round. The fact the shaft is moving tells us the motor is very likely working. I'd put this at high confidence as the coupler, with a weak motor as a much less likely second. One quick check settles it: 1. Unplug the microwave and lift the coupler straight off the shaft.
2. Look at the tip of the metal shaft. It's usually D-shaped or flatted, and it should look crisp, not chewed.
3. Plug back in, put a cup of water on the floor of the cavity (away from the bare shaft) and run it for a minute. Watch through the door window. Turntable shafts turn slowly, roughly one turn every 10 seconds or so. If it goes round steadily and smoothly, the motor is fine and the cracked coupler is the whole fault. If it only twitches, stalls or turns jerkily, the motor itself may be weak. That would be an engineer job, because the motor sits under the cavity behind the casing. Until it's sorted, the microwave is safe to keep using as long as it heats normally. Just stir or turn the food halfway through to even out the cold spots.
ok will try lifting it off the shaft. is it just a case of buying a new coupler then? model is R272WM if that helps

[Heading: Likely cause: turntable coupler]
Very likely, yes. It's a cheap, push-on part. You lift the old one off and press the new one onto the shaft, so no tools and no opening the casing. The one thing worth doing before you order is the bare-shaft check you're about to try. If the shaft goes round steadily on its own, the coupler is the whole fault. If it only twitches or stalls, the motor may be weak too, and a new coupler alone won't fix it. On getting the right one: R272WM looks like it could be a Sharp model, but I couldn't confirm an exact parts match for it, so please don't buy on my say-so. Couplers vary in the shape of the centre hole and the prong spacing.
1. Check the rating plate. It's usually inside the door frame or on the back. Confirm the full model number there, since there's often an extra letter or suffix.
2. Search the manufacturer's spares site, or a reputable spares supplier, using that exact model number. Their compatibility list is what to trust.
3. If you can, compare the listing photo with your old coupler: the hole shape (often D-shaped) and the number and position of the prongs. If you can't find a confirmed match, an appliance engineer or spares shop can identify it from the old part. That's worth doing rather than guessing. Given the cost of a coupler, it's well worth repairing rather than replacing the microwave. The only time I'd weigh up a new one is if the bare shaft turns out not to rotate properly, because a motor needs the casing opened by an engineer.
ok cheers, found the model on the label at the back, its R272WM so same as I said. will check the shaft then order a coupler

[Heading: Likely cause: turntable coupler]
That sounds like a good plan. A cracked coupler with a rounded centre hole is probably the fault, and since the shaft underneath moves, the motor is very likely fine. I'd put the coupler at high confidence. One caveat on ordering: even with R272WM confirmed from the rating plate, I couldn't find a confirmed parts match for that exact model, so I can't point you to a specific coupler. The safest routes are:
1. Search the manufacturer's own spares site (it looks likely to be a Sharp) using R272WM. If it's listed there, that's the one to trust.
2. If not, use a reputable spares supplier's model search, and compare the photo with your old coupler: the centre hole shape and the number and spacing of the prongs.
3. If you still can't find a confirmed match, take the old coupler to a spares shop or ask an appliance engineer to identify it. Don't buy a "universal" one on a guess, because a loose fit will just slip again. When you do the bare-shaft check, a steady, slow rotation means the new coupler should fix it completely. If the shaft only twitches or stalls, hold off on the coupler and get an engineer to look at the motor. That sits behind the casing, so it isn't one to do yourself.
